title: Baba in Wonderland: Online Self-Supervised Dynamics Discovery for Executable World Models
claim: Remapping semantic labels removes lexical shortcuts, so prediction errors during exploration drive successive, interpretable program revisions.
layout: Left setup column, right three stacked rows, left-to-right, dashed arrows
description: The left column shows a Default World game grid (BABA IS YOU, FLAG IS WIN) above a legend of rule objects, then a down arrow to Baba in Wonderland. There the same grid carries unrelated words (STRANGE, SHRINK, EAT), with a remapping panel showing YOU→STRANGE, WIN→SHRINK and STOP→EAT. Dashed arrows lead to three horizontal rows on the right. Each row has four stages joined by black arrows: Exploration Start, Predicted Transition, Actual Transition and Program Update. The first three are dark game-grid screenshots with yellow arrows marking the agent's move. The last is a dark code box with a Python step function and a bold banner such as 'The wall is an obstacle!!'. A yellow caption bar under each row explains why the prediction error triggers an update. The eye goes first to the colorful grids and the code boxes.
caption: Alice in Baba in Wonderland. Left: simulator dynamics are preserved while rule-property labels are semantically remapped, removing lexical shortcuts. Right: exploration exposes prediction errors that drive successive executable world-model revisions.
abstract: Executable world models can be read, edited, executed, and reused for planning, but only if the program captures the environment's transition law rather than semantic shortcuts in its surface vocabulary. We study online executable world-model learning under prior misalignment, where an agent must induce state-dependent dynamics from interaction evidence alone, without rule descriptions, reward signals, or trustworthy lexical priors. We introduce Alice, a closed-loop system that treats failed candidate updates as structural signal: when a candidate explains a new transition but loses previously explained ones, the preservation conflict reveals dynamics that the current program had conflated. Alice refines these conflicts into hypothesis classes that both provide a few broken examples, one per affected class, for update and guide frontier exploration toward transitions that are novel and underrepresented with respect to the current program. We evaluate Alice on Baba in Wonderland, a prior-misaligned variant of Baba Is You that preserves simulator dynamics while replacing semantically meaningful rule-property labels with unrelated words. Experiments show that Alice substantially improves executable world-model learning under prior misalignment, and five-run ablations support overall improvement trends as class structure and exploration signals are added. Project page: https://ssw03270.github.io/BABAinWonderland_NeurIPS-26_Page/.
